lessonTitle: Icebergs: Frozen Giants with Stories to Tell
level: OFS Grade 9 International English G1/G2 ESL
lessonGoal: Students explain how icebergs form, how ice cores preserve evidence about the past, and how scientists use that evidence to understand Earth’s climate, then write a cautious evidence-based science explanation.

pages.title: Icebergs: Frozen Giants with Stories to Tell

paragraphs: They may look like just big blocks of ice, but icebergs are full of surprises! These frozen giants float across oceans and hide most of their size underwater. Ready to dive into the chilly world of icebergs?

sections.heading: How Do Icebergs Form?
paragraphs: Icebergs begin as tiny snowflakes! Over hundreds or even thousands of years, snow builds up pressing down into thick, heavy glaciers. When a piece of that glacier breaks off and crashes into the sea, it becomes an iceberg: a giant chunk of floating ice!
But here’s the wild part: only about 10% of the iceberg floats above the water. The other 90% is hidden below, like a frozen secret!

sections.heading: What Can We Learn From Icebergs?
paragraphs: Icebergs aren’t just frozen water. They’re frozen history.

Some icebergs break off from glaciers that are thousands of years old. As snow built up long ago, it trapped tiny bubbles of air, dust, and even ash from volcanoes. Over time, that snow turned into tightly packed ice.
Scientists drill deep into glaciers to collect long tubes called ice cores: rods made of ice. These icy layers are like pages in a history book:
bullets: The deeper the layer, the older the air inside.
Scientists can measure gases like carbon dioxide (CO₂) to see how clean or polluted the air was.
They can even spot layers with volcanic ash, which helps them know when volcanoes erupted — even ones from thousands of years ago!
paragraphsAfterBullets: By studying these layers, scientists can:
secondaryBullets: See how Earth’s climate has changed
Compare ancient air to today’s air
Understand how fast the planet is warming

sections.heading: How Many Icebergs Are Out There?
paragraphs: There are tens of thousands of icebergs floating in the oceans and many are bigger than cities! Most come from the icy lands of Antarctica and Greenland.

Every year, around 15,000 to 30,000 icebergs break off just from Greenland’s glaciers. In Antarctica, some icebergs are so massive they’re named and tracked by satellite. One iceberg, called A-76, was over 4,300 square kilometers (that’s bigger than Rhode Island!).

mainIdeaQuestion.question: What is the main idea of the two-page visual text?
options: Icebergs are only beautiful objects and cannot tell scientists anything.
Icebergs form from glaciers, preserve evidence in their layers, and help scientists study Earth’s history and climate.
Every iceberg is exactly the same size and comes from Greenland.
Scientists can learn about the future only by measuring ocean waves.

feedback.correct: Correct! Option B accurately captures the main idea across both pages: icebergs originate from compressed glacier ice, trap historical air and particles in their layers, and enable scientists to examine past climate conditions.
feedback.incorrect: Incorrect. Re-read both pages of the visual text. The text highlights how icebergs form from glaciers, contain historical bubbles and ash, and allow scientists to analyze Earth's climate history.

mainIdeaQuestion.explanation: Option B is correct because the visual text combines two key themes across both pages: the physical formation, submerged nature, and scale of icebergs (glaciers, 10% visible, Greenland/Antarctica) and the scientific value of ice layers and ice cores in revealing Earth's climate history.

evidenceFromText.title: Evidence from the Text
evidenceFromText.instructions: Answer each question thoroughly using specific facts and details from the visual text. Check your response and compare it with the model answer.

prompts.statement: What details explain how an iceberg forms and why most of it is hidden underwater?
prompts.modelAnswer: According to the visual text, icebergs begin as tiny snowflakes that accumulate over hundreds or thousands of years, pressing down into thick, heavy glaciers. When a section of the glacier breaks off and crashes into the sea, it becomes a floating iceberg. The source notes that only about 10% floats above the surface, while the remaining 90% is hidden beneath the water.
prompts.compareTips: Check that your response mentions: (1) snowflakes compressing over hundreds/thousands of years into glaciers, (2) a piece breaking off into the ocean, and (3) the 10% visible / 90% underwater ratio.

prompts.statement: What evidence shows that ice layers can preserve information about the past?
prompts.modelAnswer: The text explains that ancient snow trapped tiny bubbles of air, dust, and volcanic ash as it turned into tightly packed ice. When scientists extract ice cores—long rods of ice drilled from deep inside glaciers—they can examine these distinct layers. The deeper layers hold older air, allowing researchers to measure trapped carbon dioxide (CO₂) and identify volcanic eruptions from thousands of years ago.
prompts.compareTips: Verify that your answer cites: (1) trapped air bubbles, dust, or volcanic ash, (2) ice cores collected from glaciers, and (3) deeper layers preserving older air and historical CO₂ levels.

prompts.statement: How does the second image show that icebergs can vary greatly in number and size?
prompts.modelAnswer: The second page reports that tens of thousands of icebergs float across the oceans, many being larger than cities. Greenland alone produces approximately 15,000 to 30,000 new icebergs each year. Furthermore, in Antarctica, some are massive enough to be tracked by satellite, such as iceberg A-76, which measured over 4,300 square kilometers—an area larger than Rhode Island.
prompts.compareTips: Ensure your answer includes: (1) tens of thousands in the oceans, (2) 15,000 to 30,000 breaking off from Greenland yearly, and (3) massive satellite-tracked icebergs like A-76 exceeding 4,300 square kilometers.

languageFocus.title: Language Focus
languageFocus.instructions: Examine the grammatical structures and analytical patterns below to improve your science explanation writing.

patterns.name: Time and Process
patterns.pattern: Over hundreds or even thousands of years, [Subject] + [Verb] ...
patterns.explanation: Used to describe gradual geological and atmospheric changes that unfold over extensive eras.
patterns.example: Over hundreds or even thousands of years, snow builds up pressing down into thick, heavy glaciers.

patterns.name: Cause and Result Clauses
patterns.explanation: Connects an environmental trigger directly to its physical outcome.
patterns.example: When a piece of that glacier breaks off and crashes into the sea, it becomes an iceberg.

patterns.name: Quantity and Approximation
patterns.pattern: about [Number]% / around [Number] to [Number] / tens of thousands
patterns.explanation: Enables cautious reporting of scientific estimates rather than presenting approximations as absolute figures.
patterns.example: Around 15,000 to 30,000 icebergs break off just from Greenland’s glaciers every year.

patterns.name: Proportional Comparative Pattern
patterns.pattern: The [Comparative adjective] the [Noun], the [Comparative adjective] the [Noun] ...
patterns.explanation: Shows how two environmental variables change in direct relationship to each other.
patterns.example: The deeper the layer, the older the air inside.

patterns.name: Purpose Infinitives
patterns.pattern: [Verb phrase] + to see / to understand [Noun clause / Question word clause]
patterns.explanation: Expresses the scientific objective or research goal behind an observational method.
patterns.example: Scientists can measure gases like carbon dioxide (CO₂) to see how clean or polluted the air was.

patterns.name: Source Attribution & Cautious Claims
patterns.pattern: According to the visual source, ... / The text states that ...
patterns.explanation: Accurately attributes data to the classroom visual document rather than claiming personal certainty.
patterns.example: According to the visual source, only about 10% of an iceberg floats above the water.

writingPractice.title: Writing Practice
writingPractice.instructions: Complete each guided writing exercise using the target language patterns and source details. Check and compare your answer with the model response.

prompts.question: Write a process sentence explaining how a glacier can become an iceberg.
prompts.modelAnswer: Over hundreds or thousands of years, accumulated snow presses down into a thick glacier until a piece breaks off and crashes into the sea as a floating iceberg.
prompts.compareTips: Include process markers (such as 'over thousands of years', 'presses down', or 'when... breaks off') to describe the transition from snow/glacier to iceberg.

prompts.question: Combine the 10% and 90% information using while or whereas.
prompts.modelAnswer: While only about 10% of an iceberg floats visibly above the ocean surface, approximately 90% remains hidden beneath the water.
prompts.compareTips: Use 'while' or 'whereas' to contrast the small visible portion (about 10%) with the submerged majority (about 90%).

prompts.question: Write an evidence sentence about air, dust or volcanic ash in ice layers.
prompts.modelAnswer: As ancient snow turned into tightly packed ice, it trapped bubbles of air, dust, and volcanic ash that reveal when historical eruptions occurred.
prompts.compareTips: Mention what is trapped (air bubbles, dust, or volcanic ash) and how it preserves historical evidence.

prompts.question: Write a cautious conclusion explaining why ice cores can help scientists understand climate change.
prompts.modelAnswer: By measuring ancient gases like carbon dioxide in ice cores, scientists can cautiously evaluate how Earth’s climate changed over time and how fast the planet is currently warming.
prompts.compareTips: Use cautious language (such as 'can help', 'evaluate', or 'suggest') connecting ice-core gas measurements to climate change.

writingTask.title: Final Writing Task
writingTask.prompt: How can icebergs and ice cores help us understand Earth’s history and climate? Write an evidence-based explanation paragraph of 100–140 words. Explain how icebergs form, use at least three accurate details from the visual source, describe one kind of evidence preserved in ice, and end with a cautious statement about what scientists can learn.
checklist: Clear controlling idea introducing icebergs and historical climate evidence
Accurate formation explanation describing snow compression and breaking off
At least three exact details from the visual source (e.g., 10%/90%, timeframes, Greenland/Antarctica figures)
At least one specific kind of evidence preserved in ice (air bubbles, CO₂, or volcanic ash)
Clear connection between ice-core layers and Earth's climate history
Accurate evidence-reporting phrase (e.g., 'According to the visual source...')
Cautious language for interpretation (e.g., 'suggests', 'helps evaluate', 'can indicate')
Logical concluding sentence summarizing scientific learning
Word count strictly between 100 and 140 words
writingTask.modelAnswer: Icebergs begin as tiny snowflakes that compress over hundreds or thousands of years into thick, heavy glaciers. When a section of a glacier breaks off and crashes into the ocean, it becomes a floating iceberg with only about 10% visible above water while 90% remains hidden. According to the visual source, these frozen giants preserve valuable history because ancient ice trapped tiny bubbles of air, dust, and volcanic ash. By drilling cylindrical ice cores deep into glaciers, scientists can measure historical gases such as carbon dioxide (CO₂) within the sequential layers. Consequently, these preserved samples enable researchers to cautiously evaluate historical atmospheric patterns, compare ancient air with modern conditions, and better understand how rapidly the global climate is warming.

selfCheck.title: Self-Check
selfCheck.instructions: Review your written paragraph against the checklist below before submitting your work.
items: I explained how snow compresses into a glacier and breaks off into an iceberg.
I cited at least three specific details from the visual source (e.g., 10%/90%, timeframes, Greenland/Antarctica).
I clearly described one type of evidence preserved in ice (air bubbles, CO₂, or volcanic ash).
I explained how ice cores connect to understanding Earth's climate history.
I used cautious reporting expressions (such as 'suggests', 'indicates', or 'can help evaluate').
My paragraph is organized with a clear topic sentence, supporting evidence, and a conclusion within 100–140 words.

rubric.excellent: Thoroughly explains iceberg formation, identifies trapped atmospheric evidence, and makes a cautious, thoughtful connection to climate science using rich source details.
rubric.developing: Explains iceberg formation and mentions ice core evidence, but details may be general or the climate connection partially developed.
rubric.beginning: Struggles to clearly explain formation or historical evidence; relies on incomplete or inaccurate source details.

rubric.excellent: Accurately integrates at least three specific source details (e.g., 10%/90%, timeframes, Greenland/Antarctica scale) and describes ice-core evidence with precision.
rubric.developing: Includes two accurate source details; references evidence but may describe it somewhat vaguely without citing specific gases or particles.
rubric.beginning: Cites fewer than two source details or misstates numbers and percentages from the visual text.

rubric.excellent: Skillfully employs process clauses ('Over hundreds of years...', 'When... breaks off'), contrast markers ('while/whereas'), and cautious attribution phrases ('According to the visual...').

rubric.developing: Follows a recognizable paragraph structure with topic, body, and conclusion, though transitions between formation and evidence may be abrupt.
rubric.beginning: Lacks paragraph coherence; ideas jump randomly between iceberg size, formation, and climate without a logical sequence.

rubric.excellent: Maintains high grammatical and lexical accuracy; correctly reproduces chemical notations (CO₂) and numerical figures within 100–140 words.
rubric.developing: Minor errors in verb tenses, prepositions, or singular/plural agreements that do not impede overall comprehension.
rubric.beginning: Frequent errors in sentence boundaries, word order, or numerical data that obscure scientific meaning.

teacherNotes: 1. Visual Source Layout: The lesson is based on two teacher-provided classroom visual text images. Image 1 covers iceberg formation, submerged volume, and ice core evidence. Image 2 covers global distribution and massive scale.
2. Locked Source Fidelity: All 320 main prose and list words, 3 headings, and 14 visual labels are preserved verbatim. No external publications, URLs, or invented authors are added.

3. The 10% / 90% Principle: Emphasize the physical reality of iceberg buoyancy—roughly 10% above water and 90% submerged—which illustrates why icebergs are described as 'hiding most of their size underwater.'
4. Glacial Time Scales: Highlight the immense duration ('hundreds or even thousands of years') required for fluffy snowflakes to compress under pressure into solid glacial ice.
5. Ice Cores as Historical Archives: Teach students the metaphor 'pages in a history book'—each annual layer represents a snapshot of past atmospheric conditions and volcanic activity.
6. Chemical Notation CO₂: Ensure students understand that carbon dioxide is denoted as CO₂, representing ancient atmospheric gas trapped in pressurized ice bubbles.
7. Volcanic Ash Layers: Explain that distinct dark ash bands serve as geological time markers, enabling scientists to date major eruptions thousands of years ago.
8. Geographic Origins: Reinforce that the primary sources of ocean icebergs are Antarctica and Greenland, with Greenland releasing 15,000–30,000 icebergs annually.
9. Distinguishing Source Claims from Universal Truths: Students should recognize that figures like 'A-76 was over 4,300 square kilometers' are specific historical observations reported in the source.
10. ESL Scaffolding for G1/G2 Learners: Provide sentence frames for process explanation and contrast ('While X floats, Y is hidden') to support developing bilingual writers.
11. Respectful Climate Discourse: Encourage cautious scientific interpretations—highlighting that ice cores allow scientists to 'understand how fast the planet is warming' without sensationalism.

teachingScript.objective: Activate curiosity about icebergs and establish the 90-minute learning target.
actions: Display the title 'Icebergs: Frozen Giants with Stories to Tell' on the board.
State the lesson goal clearly in English and Korean.
Check students' readiness to explore polar science concepts.
teachingScript.teacherTalk: Welcome class! Today we explore 'Icebergs: Frozen Giants with Stories to Tell.' Our goal today is to explain how icebergs form, how ice cores preserve ancient Earth history, and write an evidence-based paragraph.
teachingScript.script: Teacher: 'Good morning everyone! Take a look at our title today: Icebergs: Frozen Giants with Stories to Tell. (안녕하세요 여러분! 오늘 우리는 '빙산: 이야기를 간직한 얼음 거인들'을 공부합니다.) Today we will discover how snowflakes turn into giant floating icebergs and how ancient air bubbles help scientists study Earth's climate history. By the end of our 90 minutes, you will write a complete science explanation paragraph.'
teachingScript.studentActions: Listen attentively, open their student interface, and write down the lesson goal.
teachingScript.misconception: Students might assume icebergs are just frozen seawater formed directly from freezing waves.
teachingScript.feedback: Remind students that icebergs originate from compressed land snow on glaciers, not frozen salty seawater.
teachingScript.transition: Now, let's explore what you already know in our Warm-up discussion.

teachingScript.objective: Engage prior knowledge on polar environments, glaciers, and historical evidence.
actions: Direct students to the 3 warm-up prompts.
Facilitate pair sharing for 4 minutes.
Elicit responses from 3–4 student volunteers.
teachingScript.teacherTalk: Look at the three warm-up questions. Turn to your partner and share what you know about Antarctica, why ice might trap old information, and how scientists use evidence.

teachingScript.misconception: Students may think ice melts and refreezes every year, destroying any historical records.
teachingScript.feedback: Explain that in polar glaciers, cold temperatures allow ice layers to accumulate continuously without melting for thousands of years.
teachingScript.transition: Let's master the 10 essential scientific vocabulary words we will encounter in the text.

teachingScript.objective: Build precise scientific vocabulary needed for comprehension and writing.
actions: Present the 10 target vocabulary words with definitions and Korean meanings.
Model correct pronunciation and intonation.
Have students read example sentences aloud.
teachingScript.teacherTalk: We have 10 key terms today: iceberg, glacier, press down, break off, float, hidden, ice core, layer, volcanic ash, and climate. Notice that 'ice core' is a long rod of ice collected by drilling deep into a glacier.
teachingScript.script: Teacher: 'Repeat after me: ice core / a long tube of ice / drilled from a glacier. (빙하 코어는 빙하 깊은 곳을 시추하여 수집한 긴 얼음 원통입니다.) When snow presses down over thousands of years, it traps air bubbles. This is how ice cores become frozen history books.'

teachingScript.misconception: Students might confuse 'iceberg' (floating chunk) with 'glacier' (massive land ice sheet).

actions: Deconstruct the 6 target language patterns on the board.
Model how to combine clauses using 'while/whereas'.
Conduct quick choral drills on proportional comparative: 'The deeper the layer, the older the air.'
teachingScript.teacherTalk: Notice how scientists express proportional relationships: 'The deeper the layer, the older the air inside.' Notice also how we report numbers cautiously using 'around' and 'about.'
teachingScript.script: Teacher: 'Let's practice the proportional comparative: The deeper the layer / the older the air inside. (층이 더 깊을수록 / 그 안의 공기는 더 오래되었습니다.) This pattern shows a direct cause-and-effect relationship in ice core stratigraphy.'
teachingScript.studentActions: Identify patterns in the text, take notes on sentence frames, and practice oral transformations.
teachingScript.misconception: Students often write 'The deeper layer is older' instead of using the paired correlative 'The deeper..., the older...'.
teachingScript.feedback: Reinforce the double comparative structure: 'The + comparative, the + comparative.'
teachingScript.transition: Now let's apply these sentence patterns in our guided Writing Practice.

teachingScript.objective: Complete 4 Writing Practice items and construct a 100–140 word evidence-based science explanation paragraph.
actions: Monitor students as they complete Writing Practice 1–4.
Review the Final Writing Task checklist and prompt criteria.
Provide individual feedback and enforce the 100–140 word requirement.
teachingScript.teacherTalk: Complete Writing Practice 1 through 4. Then begin your Final Writing Task. Your paragraph must be 100 to 140 words, explain formation, cite three source details, describe ice evidence, and conclude cautiously.
teachingScript.script: Teacher: 'Keep your eye on the live word count! Aim for about 120 words. Make sure you use cautious language like 'helps scientists understand' rather than declaring absolute certainty.'
teachingScript.studentActions: Draft WP1–WP4, write their final explanation paragraph, check word count, and run the Writing Check tool.
teachingScript.misconception: Students might write fewer than 100 words or omit the connection between ice cores and climate change.
teachingScript.feedback: Encourage students to expand by explaining what trapped CO₂ and volcanic ash tell researchers about ancient air.
teachingScript.transition: Let's finalize our work with Self-Check and submit our responses.

teachingScript.objective: Review the 6-point checklist, confirm complete work, and submit the lesson.
actions: Direct students to check off all 6 Self-Check items.
Ensure student name and student code are filled in.
Verify successful submission status in the system.
teachingScript.teacherTalk: Check all six items in your Self-Check list. When ready, enter your name and student code, and click Submit. Excellent job exploring Earth's frozen giants today!
teachingScript.script: Teacher: 'Before clicking submit, confirm: Did you explain formation? Did you mention CO₂ or ash? Is your word count between 100 and 140? Click submit now! (제출 버튼을 누르기 전 6가지 자가 점검 항목을 확인하세요.) Great work today, class!'
teachingScript.studentActions: Check off the 6 Self-Check criteria, input their identification, and submit their lesson work.
teachingScript.misconception: Students might submit without reviewing the checklist or checking their word count.
teachingScript.feedback: Remind students that the rule-based writing check gives immediate feedback on paragraph structure.
teachingScript.transition: Class dismissed! Next lesson we will explore another exciting environmental science feature.

warmupGuide.question: What do you already know about icebergs, glaciers or Antarctica?

warmupGuide.purpose: Establish evidence-based reasoning as the core methodology for the writing task.

Ice cores reveal atmospheric gas concentrations from past eras.

teachingTranscript.korean: 본문은 '빙하 코어라 불리는 긴 원통: 얼음으로 만들어진 막대기'라고 설명합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: What literary device is used here? A simile: 'like pages in a history book.'
teachingTranscript.korean: 여기서 사용된 문학적 장치는 무엇인가요? 바로 직유입니다: '역사책 속의 페이지들처럼.'

teachingTranscript.english: Notice the colon at the end. It signals that the following three bullets explain how to read these pages!
teachingTranscript.korean: 끝부분의 콜론에 주목하세요. 뒤따르는 세 개의 글머리 기호가 이 페이지들을 어떻게 읽는지를 설명한다는 신호입니다!

teachingTranscript.english: This is one of our target language structures: 'The deeper the layer, the older the air inside.'
teachingTranscript.korean: 이것이 우리의 목표 언어 구문 중 하나입니다: '층이 더 깊을수록, 그 안의 공기는 더 오래되었습니다.'

teachingTranscript.english: Why is deeper air older? Because new snow always falls on top of older layers.
teachingTranscript.korean: 왜 더 깊은 곳의 공기가 더 오래되었을까요? 새로운 눈이 항상 오래된 층 위에 내리기 때문입니다.

sentences.original: Scientists can measure gases like carbon dioxide (CO₂) to see how clean or polluted the air was.

mustKnowChunks.example: Plants absorb carbon dioxide (CO₂) during photosynthesis.
Tests were run to see how effective the medicine was.

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: Infinitive of purpose 'to see' governing an embedded interrogative complement clause 'how clean or polluted the air was'.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: When scientists melt tiny bits of ice in a vacuum, the trapped air bubbles pop! / They test the air for gases like carbon dioxide (CO₂). / This tells them how much greenhouse gas was in the air thousands of years ago. / They can compare past air with today's air.

teachingTranscript.english: Pay close attention to the chemical formula here: CO₂ with a subscript 2.
teachingTranscript.korean: 여기의 화학식에 주의를 기울이세요: 아래 첨자 2가 붙은 CO₂입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: By measuring CO₂, scientists can reconstruct past atmospheres without guessing.
teachingTranscript.korean: CO₂를 측정함으로써 과학자들은 추측하지 않고도 과거의 대기를 재구성할 수 있습니다.

sentences.original: They can even spot layers with volcanic ash, which helps them know when volcanoes erupted — even ones from thousands of years ago!

sentences.naturalKorean: 심지어 화산재가 섞인 층을 발견할 수도 있는데, 이는 수천 년 전에 일어난 화산 폭발의 시기까지도 파악하는 데 도움을 줍니다!

mustKnowChunks.example: Researchers easily spotted layers containing dark soil.

Fossil evidence helps them know how ancient animals moved.

commonMistakes.correction: Ice cores are long cylinders or rods of ice collected by drilling deep into glaciers.
